defaults.source: Widely published whakataukī; explanations written by AI for this app from commonly published accounts. Not yet reviewed by a fluent speaker or cultural advisor.

items.title: He aha te mea nui o te ao?

lines.mi: He aha te mea nui o te ao?
lines.en: What is the most important thing in the world?

lines.mi: He tangata, he tangata, he tangata.
lines.en: It is people, it is people, it is people.

items.literal: What [is] the great thing of the world? A person, a person, a person.
items.meaning: People and relationships matter more than possessions, status or achievements. The threefold repetition gives the answer weight and finality.
items.provenance: Commonly attributed to Meri Ngāroto, a woman of rank of Te Aupōuri in the Far North. These lines are the close of a longer saying that begins 'Hutia te rito o te harakeke, kei hea te kōmako e kō?' (If the centre shoot of the flax is pulled out, where will the bellbird sing?). Accounts of the exact circumstances differ between sources.
items.context: In the longer saying, the rito (centre shoot) of the harakeke stands for the child, protected by the surrounding leaves as parents and grandparents protect a child. Removing it kills the plant. The saying is about the survival of whānau and people across generations.
items.usage: Very widely quoted in speeches, education, health and public-sector settings to emphasise that people come first. Because it is so often quoted on its own, it is worth knowing that it belongs to a longer saying with its own history, and acknowledging that when you can.
items.nuances: Because someone is named as its author it is sometimes called a whakatauākī (a saying with a known originator) rather than a whakataukī. Tangata (no macron) is singular, 'a person'; some published versions use the plural tāngata. This app uses the singular form; either may be met in print.

components.note: He + aha asks what something is.
The describing word nui follows the noun mea.
o = of, belonging to.
A He sentence classifies: it is a person.

structureQs.prompt: In this whakataukī, what does 'he aha' ask?
structureQs.explain: He aha …? asks what something is.

structureQs.prompt: What does 'te mea nui' mean, word for word?
structureQs.explain: te (the) + mea (thing) + nui (big, great, important). The describing word follows the noun.
o te ao = of the world.

structureQs.prompt: Does 'tangata' (no macron) mean one person or several?
structureQs.explain: tangata = person; tāngata = people. The macron marks the plural.

items.title: Whāia te iti kahurangi

lines.en: Pursue that which is most precious;

lines.mi: ki te tūohu koe, me he maunga teitei.
lines.en: if you must bow your head, let it be to a lofty mountain.

items.literal: Pursue the precious small thing; if you bow, [let it be] as to a lofty mountain.
items.meaning: Aim for what you value most and keep going. If you have to yield, yield only to an obstacle that is truly great. It encourages high aspiration and perseverance.
items.provenance: A widely known traditional whakataukī. This app does not attribute it to a named person or iwi because no attribution could be confirmed; if you learn its origin from a reliable source, add it to the content file.
items.context: Often used to encourage learners and anyone setting out on something difficult. The image is of a traveller who lowers their head only before a great mountain, not before small obstacles.
items.usage: Common in education, graduations, farewells and messages of encouragement. Appropriate when acknowledging someone's goals or effort.
items.nuances: Iti kahurangi is an idiom: literally 'small precious thing', it refers to a treasured goal or aspiration. Kahurangi can mean precious, prized, or a prized variety of pounamu. 'Me he' means 'as if, like a', so the last phrase is literally 'as if [to] a lofty mountain'. English renderings vary.

components.note: Command form of whai (to follow, pursue). The ending -a marks the passive, which is how commands are given with verbs that take an object.

components.gloss: the precious thing; one's highest aspiration
components.note: An idiom; see the notes on interpretation.
ki te + verb = if. tūohu = to bow the head, stoop.

components.gloss: [let it be] as to a lofty mountain
components.note: me he = as if, like a. teitei = lofty, tall.

structureQs.prompt: 'Whāia' is the command form of which verb?
structureQs.explain: whai = to follow, pursue. Whāia! = Pursue (it)!

structureQs.prompt: In 'ki te tūohu koe', what does 'ki te' express?
structureQs.explain: ki te + verb introduces a condition: if you bow.
he maunga teitei = a lofty mountain. The describing word follows the noun.
tūohu = to bow the head, stoop.

items.title: Ko te reo te mauri o te mana Māori

lines.mi: Ko te reo te mauri o te mana Māori.
lines.en: The language is the life force of Māori mana.

items.literal: The language [is] the life force of the Māori mana.
items.meaning: The Māori language is what gives life to Māori identity, standing and authority. If the language is lost, what makes Māori distinct is lost with it.
items.provenance: Attributed to Tā Hēmi Hēnare (Sir James Hēnare, Ngāti Hine), and widely associated with his evidence in the Waitangi Tribunal's te reo Māori claim in the mid-1980s. Because it has a known author it is a whakatauākī.
items.context: Said in the context of the campaign for recognition and revitalisation of te reo Māori, which led to the language becoming an official language of New Zealand in 1987.
items.usage: Often quoted when speaking about the value of te reo and the reasons for learning and protecting it. Fitting for a learner to know; acknowledge its author when you use it.
items.nuances: Mauri is the life force or vital essence of a being or thing. Mana covers authority, prestige and spiritual standing, and has no single English equivalent. English renderings of this saying vary.

components.note: Ko introduces the specific thing being identified.
The second definite phrase says what the first one is.
o = of, belonging to. Māori follows mana because describing words follow the noun.

structureQs.prompt: Which word in this saying means 'life force'?
Which small word begins the sentence and identifies a specific thing?
structureQs.explain: Ko te reo … = The language is …

items.title: Ehara taku toa i te toa takitahi

lines.mi: Ehara taku toa i te toa takitahi,
lines.en: My strength is not that of one person alone;
it is the strength of many.

items.literal: My strength is not the strength of a single one, but a strength of multitudes.
items.meaning: What I achieve is not mine alone. Success comes from the support and effort of many people: whānau, colleagues, community and those who came before.
items.provenance: A widely quoted traditional saying. Published sources commonly attribute it to Paterangi of Ngāti Kahungunu; this attribution has not been independently checked for this app.
items.context: Used to acknowledge that an individual's achievement rests on a collective. It expresses the value placed on working together over individual credit.
items.usage: Common when accepting thanks or recognition, opening a team presentation, or acknowledging the people behind a piece of work.
items.nuances: Toa means bravery, strength or success, and also warrior. Taki- before a number word describes grouping: takitahi, singly; takitini, in multitudes. Some versions have 'taku toa takitini' in the second half.

components.note: Ehara … i … negates a sentence that says what something is (a Ko or He sentence).
takitahi = singly, individual.
takitini = many, in multitudes.

structureQs.prompt: Which word at the start makes the statement negative?

structureQs.explain: taku = my; toa = strength, bravery, success.

structureQs.prompt: Which word means 'singly, as one alone'?

items.title: Nāu te rourou, nāku te rourou

lines.mi: Nāu te rourou, nāku te rourou,
lines.en: With your food basket and my food basket,
the people will thrive.

items.literal: Yours the food basket, mine the food basket; by that the people will live.
items.meaning: When each person contributes what they have, everyone is sustained. It is about cooperation and pooling resources for the good of all.
items.provenance: A widely known traditional whakataukī. This app does not attribute it to a named person or iwi because no attribution could be confirmed.
items.context: The rourou is a small woven basket for cooked food. The image is of people each bringing their basket so that the whole group can eat.
items.usage: Used to encourage collaboration, to acknowledge contributions to a shared effort, and when thanking people who have each given something.
items.nuances: Nāu and nāku mean 'yours' and 'mine' in the a category, here with a sense of 'what you bring' and 'what I bring'. Ka … ai marks a result that follows from what was just said. Ora means life, health and wellbeing, so 'live', 'be well' and 'thrive' are all used in translation.

components.note: nāu = yours (one person).
nāku = mine.
ai points back to the cause: as a result of that.

structureQs.explain: A small woven basket for cooked food.

structureQs.prompt: Which word means 'live, be well, thrive'?

items.title: He waka eke noa

lines.en: A canoe that all may board; we are all in this together.

items.literal: A canoe [to be] boarded without restriction.
items.meaning: Commonly used to mean that everyone is in the same boat and shares the journey and its outcome, so everyone should pull together.
items.provenance: A well-known whakataukī of uncertain origin. This app does not attribute it to a named person or iwi.
items.context: The waka is a frequent image for a shared undertaking: everyone aboard depends on everyone else.
items.usage: Used widely for team efforts and shared challenges. Because its original sense is debated, it is worth being a little careful about leaning on one fixed English slogan for it.
items.nuances: Noa means free from restriction, ordinary, without conditions. Eke means to board, embark or mount. Some speakers explain the saying as a canoe that anyone may board without ceremony, which is not quite the same idea as 'we are all in this together'. Interpretations differ.

components.note: Follows the verb and modifies it.

structureQs.prompt: Which word means 'to board or embark'?

items.title: Mā te huruhuru ka rere te manu

lines.mi: Mā te huruhuru ka rere te manu.
lines.en: It is by feathers that the bird flies.

items.literal: By means of the feathers the bird will fly.
items.meaning: No one succeeds without the right support and resources. Give people what they need (skills, backing, funding, encouragement) and they can take flight.
items.provenance: A widely known traditional whakataukī. This app does not attribute it to a named person or iwi because no attribution could be confirmed.
items.context: The image is of a bird that cannot leave the ground until it is fully feathered. It is often rendered in English as 'Adorn the bird with feathers so it may soar'.
items.usage: Used when asking for or acknowledging support for a person or a project, in education, and when resourcing a piece of work.
items.nuances: Mā here marks the means by which something will come about. The same mā … ka shape is used in other sayings to say 'through X, Y will happen'.

components.note: mā = by means of, through. huruhuru = feathers, hair.
rere = fly, flow.

structureQs.prompt: What does 'huruhuru' mean in this saying?
Which small word at the start means 'by means of'?
structureQs.explain: Mā te huruhuru = by means of the feathers.

items.title: He kai kei aku ringa

lines.en: There is food at the end of my hands.

items.meaning: I can provide for myself by my own effort and skill. It expresses self-reliance, resilience and confidence in one's own abilities.
items.provenance: A widely known traditional whakataukī. This app does not attribute it to a named person or iwi because no attribution could be confirmed.
items.context: The hands stand for work and skill: whoever can use their hands will not go hungry.
items.usage: Used to encourage people to back their own abilities, and to acknowledge someone who has made their own way through hard work.
items.nuances: Kei marks present location, so the food is 'at' the hands. Aku is the neutral plural 'my'. English versions usually add 'at the end of' to make the image clear.

components.note: aku = my (several things).

structureQs.prompt: Which word here marks where something is now?

items.title: Ka mua, ka muri

lines.en: Looking back in order to move forward.

items.meaning: We move into the future with our eyes on the past. What has gone before is what guides what comes next.
items.provenance: A widely known traditional whakataukī. This app does not attribute it to a named person or iwi because no attribution could be confirmed.
items.context: In Māori thought the past lies in front, where it can be seen, and the future lies behind, unseen. Mua means both 'in front' and 'before in time'; muri means both 'behind' and 'afterwards'. The saying is often explained as walking backwards into the future.
items.usage: Used when acknowledging history, tūpuna or earlier work before setting out plans, and in strategy and education settings.
items.nuances: The English versions are explanations, not translations: the Māori is only four words. Its force depends on the double meaning of mua and muri.

components.note: mua = in front, before.
muri = behind, after.

structureQs.prompt: 'Mua' means 'in front'. What does it mean when speaking about time?
structureQs.explain: mua = in front, and before in time: the past is in front of us.

structureQs.prompt: In this way of seeing time, is the future in front of us or behind us?
structureQs.explain: The future is behind, unseen; the past is in front, visible.

items.title: Whaowhia te kete mātauranga

lines.en: Fill the basket of knowledge.

items.literal: Let the knowledge basket be filled.
items.meaning: Keep learning. Gather knowledge at every opportunity, as you would fill a basket.
items.provenance: A widely known traditional whakataukī. This app does not attribute it to a named person or iwi because no attribution could be confirmed.
items.context: The kete (woven basket) is a common image for holding knowledge. In well-known traditions, three baskets of knowledge were brought from the heavens for people.
items.usage: Very common in schools, training and anywhere learning is being encouraged or celebrated.
items.nuances: Whaowhia is the command form of whao (to fill, to put into a container): commands with verbs that act on something use the passive ending. Mātauranga follows kete and describes it: the knowledge basket.

components.note: From whao, to fill. The passive ending gives a command.
Describes the basket: the basket of knowledge.

structureQs.prompt: 'Whaowhia' is the command form of which verb?
structureQs.explain: whao = to fill, to put into.

items.title: Poipoia te kākano kia puāwai

lines.en: Nurture the seed and it will blossom.

items.literal: Let the seed be nurtured so that it may bloom.
items.meaning: With care and encouragement, potential is realised. It is most often said of children and learners, and of ideas in their early stages.
items.provenance: A widely known traditional whakataukī. This app does not attribute it to a named person or iwi because no attribution could be confirmed.
items.context: The seed stands for a child, a learner or a beginning; the blossom for what they can become when they are looked after.
items.usage: Common in early childhood, education and mentoring, and when launching something new that will need looking after.
items.nuances: Poipoia is the command form of poipoi (to nurture, to rock gently). Kia before puāwai expresses purpose or hoped-for result: so that it blossoms.

components.note: From poipoi, to nurture.
kia = so that, in order that. puāwai = to bloom.

items.title: Kāore te kūmara e kōrero mō tōna ake reka

lines.mi: Kāore te kūmara e kōrero mō tōna ake reka.
lines.en: The kūmara does not speak of its own sweetness.

items.literal: The kūmara does not talk about its own sweetness.
items.meaning: Be humble. Let others speak of your qualities and achievements; do not praise yourself.
items.provenance: A widely known traditional whakataukī. This app does not attribute it to a named person or iwi because no attribution could be confirmed.
items.context: The kūmara was a prized food, valued for its sweetness. It has no need to announce what everyone already knows.
items.usage: Used to remind people of the value of humility, and often said lightly when someone is uncomfortable being praised or asked to talk about themselves. Understanding it helps explain why people may be reluctant to promote themselves.
items.nuances: Kāore … e … negates a general or future action. Mō means about or concerning. Ake after tōna gives 'its own'. Reka is usually a describing word (sweet); here it is used as a noun, sweetness.

components.note: Kāore + subject + e + verb.
tōna = its; ake = own.

structureQs.prompt: Which word begins the sentence and makes it negative?
structureQs.explain: Kāore … e kōrero = does not speak.
mō tōna ake reka = about its own sweetness.

items.title: Introducing yourself (for tauiwi)
items.source: Sentence frames are standard te reo Māori. The approach of acknowledging rather than claiming landmarks follows publicly available advice for non-Māori, including advice attributed to Keri Opai. Written by AI; check your final wording with a kaiako or mana whenua before using it formally.

lines.en: My ancestors are from {origin}.
I was born in {born}.
I grew up in {raised}.
I live in {home}.

lines.mi: E mihi ana ki ngā tohu o nehe, o {acknowledge} e noho nei au.
lines.en: I acknowledge the ancient landmarks of {acknowledge}, where I live.
My name is {name}.

lines.mi: Nō reira, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā tātou katoa.
lines.en: Therefore, greetings to you all, greetings to us all.

slots.label: Where your ancestors are from
slots.hint: A country or region, in Māori if you know the name, e.g. Ingarangi (England), Kōtirana (Scotland), Airani (Ireland). Join several with 'me' (and).

slots.label: Where you were born
slots.hint: Use the Māori place name where one exists, e.g. Ōtautahi, Tāmaki Makaurau.

slots.label: Where you grew up
slots.hint: Leave blank to omit this line.

slots.label: Place whose landmarks you acknowledge
slots.hint: Usually the same as where you live. Leave blank to omit this line. Confirm this line with a kaiako before using it.

items.meaning: A short introduction that says where your people come from, where you were born and live, and who you are, and that acknowledges the place you live in without claiming it.
items.provenance: Pepeha is a Māori way of introducing yourself through your connections to people and places. For Māori it expresses whakapapa: the maunga, awa, waka, iwi, hapū and marae a person descends from and belongs to.
items.context: Statements such as 'Ko … tōku maunga' express an ancestral relationship with that mountain. A common view, though not the only one, is that people without that whakapapa should not claim a maunga or awa as theirs simply because they live nearby or feel attached to it. Instead, tauiwi can say where their ancestors come from, where they were born and live, and acknowledge the landmarks and people of the place they live in.
items.usage: Used when introducing yourself in a mihi, for example at the start of a hui or a course. Views on the right form for tauiwi differ between iwi, kaiako and organisations. Ask your kaiako, or mana whenua where you live, and follow their guidance over this app. This module never fills in places or connections for you.
items.nuances: Tūpuna and tīpuna (ancestors) are dialect variants; use whichever is used where you live. Nō indicates belonging to or coming from a place. The acknowledgement line is optional and is the one most worth confirming before use.

components.note: nō = from, belonging to. ōku = my (several things). tūpuna = ancestors.
whānau as a verb means to be born. mai = towards the speaker.
tipu = grow. ake = upwards.
Kei + place = at. e … ana marks an ongoing action.

components.mi: E mihi ana ki ngā tohu o nehe
components.gloss: [I] acknowledge the landmarks of ancient times
components.note: mihi = greet, acknowledge. tohu = sign, landmark. nehe = ancient times.
Ko identifies a specific name.

components.mi: Nō reira, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā tātou katoa
components.gloss: therefore, greetings to you all, greetings to us all
components.note: A standard way to close a mihi. katoa = all.

structureQs.prompt: Which word at the start of a sentence means 'from / belonging to' a place?
structureQs.explain: Nō Ingarangi ōku tūpuna = My ancestors are from England.
Ko … tōku ingoa = My name is …

structureQs.prompt: What does 'I whānau mai au i …' say?
structureQs.explain: whānau as a verb = to be born.

structureQs.prompt: Which word in the closing line means 'all'?
structureQs.explain: tēnā tātou katoa = greetings to us all.
